part_title: Lambda Data Pipelines, Kinesis Batches, Bedrock and API Integrations

scenes.title: Lambda as a data pipeline step
scenes.narration: This slide shows Lambda acting as a small but important stage in a data pipeline. Follow the top flow: new data arrives in S3 or Kinesis, that event triggers Lambda, and Lambda transforms the record before writing it to a destination such as S3. Now look at the two JSON examples in the middle. The raw customer interaction contains fields like user ID, event type, page path, referrer and timestamp. The transformed event uses a consistent analytics-friendly structure, including fields such as customer ID and action. That change is useful because downstream reports shouldn't need to understand every source application's naming conventions. The bottom panels divide responsibilities. A trigger is where the new work comes from. A destination is where the transformed output goes. They can be different services, even when both happen to be S3. Lambda performs bounded tasks: normalising fields, filtering unnecessary records, enriching values and routing the result. Larger analytics work belongs downstream, where Athena can query the data, Redshift can warehouse it, EMR can process large datasets, or QuickSight can visualise it. The important lesson is that a function can prepare data for analytics without becoming the entire analytics platform.

scenes.title: Load new data into Redshift
scenes.narration: Now imagine a sales CSV file arriving in S3. The upper diagram follows four stages. First, the new file is stored in S3. Its object-created event triggers Lambda. Lambda checks the file's format and schema and prepares a Redshift load. Redshift then runs a COPY operation to load the data from S3 in bulk. Watch the distinction between starting the load and performing the load. Lambda acts as the coordinator; Redshift is the service that moves and organises the warehouse data. The example execution log at the bottom makes the sequence concrete: the object is detected, its schema is validated, the COPY begins, and eventually the load completes. Those times show separate stages rather than one mysterious processing step. The left-hand explanation reminds us not to write a Lambda loop that inserts every CSV row into Redshift one by one. For a large dataset, bulk loading is the better fit. Lambda can log the outcome and manage errors, while longer or multi-stage operations may require orchestration beyond a single function execution. When troubleshooting, ask which stage failed: event notification, file validation, COPY permissions or the actual data load.

scenes.title: Kinesis to Lambda, batch by batch
scenes.narration: This slide shows exactly how a Kinesis stream reaches Lambda. Start on the left with the stream's shards. In the middle, a Lambda event source mapping polls those shards and groups records into batches. It then invokes the Lambda batch processor. The processor handles the records and writes results to DynamoDB, shown as the example destination. Look closely at the sample batch: several order records arrive together, while the destination table shows processed order IDs and timestamps. A stable order ID helps make these writes idempotent. Now move to the numbered scenarios below the architecture. First, the event source mapping builds a batch. If the invocation succeeds, its checkpoint can advance past the processed records. If the invocation fails, the affected records may be retried. The last case shows partial batch failure reporting, where supported: rather than making every successful record run again, the function identifies failed record IDs so processing can resume at the appropriate point. Kinesis also has ordering behavior within a shard, so retries can affect progress. The key learning point is that Lambda isn't individually pushed every stream record; its mapping manages polling, batching, checkpoints and retry behavior.

scenes.title: Lambda in a Bedrock application
scenes.narration: Let's follow a customer asking, 'What's the shipment status for order twelve million three hundred forty-five thousand six hundred seventy-eight?' The client submits that question through API Gateway, which invokes Lambda. On this slide, Lambda is the validation and tool-adapter layer between the user and Amazon Bedrock. It checks the order ID, applies business rules and calls the internal shipment system. The example tool result in the lower panel includes the order identifier, status 'In transit', carrier UPS and an estimated delivery date. Lambda formats that structured result so a Bedrock model or agent can use it. The illustrative model answer then says the package is in transit and explains the delivery estimate in natural language. Notice where the facts came from: a business system, not an invented model response. This is what makes the example valuable. The bottom panels reinforce three operational safeguards. Give Lambda the least-privilege permissions it needs, configure sensible timeouts, and handle invalid order IDs or unavailable shipment systems gracefully. Bedrock can make the response conversational, but Lambda is responsible for connecting the model to authoritative application data.

scenes.title: Build a serverless REST API
scenes.narration: Here the screen shows a complete REST API for summarising meeting notes. Start with the request at the left: the client calls POST slash summaries and sends text. API Gateway receives that request, applies the configured authentication or authoriser and throttling controls, then routes it to Lambda. Lambda checks the supplied text, prepares a prompt, invokes Bedrock and formats the result. Bedrock generates a short summary, which returns through Lambda and API Gateway as a JSON response. The lower request and response panels make this concrete. The request includes meeting text; the response has a summary field stating that the meeting covered results and next steps. Trace the numbered sequence in the lower area rather than treating the four service icons as interchangeable. API Gateway controls HTTP access and routing. Lambda implements business logic and response shaping. Bedrock produces the natural-language summary. One important clarification: API keys and usage plans can meter or identify application clients, but they are not a substitute for user authentication and authorisation. This pattern is suitable for bounded, interactive inference. If summarisation takes too long, use an asynchronous job instead of making the browser wait indefinitely.

scenes.title: API Gateway integration choices
scenes.narration: This slide compares three ways API Gateway can connect a client to a backend. Read the panels left to right. In a Lambda integration, the gateway invokes a function that can combine records, validate complex inputs or transform the response. It's useful when the application needs custom logic, as in an orders API. The middle panel is an HTTP integration. Here API Gateway forwards the request to an existing HTTP service, whether that backend runs in AWS or another reachable environment. Use it when you already have a service that can handle the request. On the right, an AWS service integration calls an eligible AWS action directly. The example uses a CloudWatch API operation, avoiding a Lambda hop that would otherwise only forward a request. Notice the sample responses beneath each panel: they look different because the backend responsibilities differ. The choice depends on what processing is needed, not which integration appears newest. Direct integrations can simplify a simple pass-through workflow, but request mappings and IAM permissions still must be correct. Lambda becomes valuable when you need business rules or richer transformation. An HTTP integration is appropriate when the logic already exists in a separate backend.
